question.problem:
What is the first term that exceeds  $1\,000$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
\sqrt{2},\,2,\,2\sqrt{2},\,4,\,…
$$

The first term that exceeds $1\,000$ is the
{{field-1}}th term.
question.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=\sqrt{2}$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot {(\sqrt{2})}^{n-1} \\  & ={2}^{n/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $1\,000.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & >1\,000 \\ {2}^{n/2} & >1\,000 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({2}^{n/2}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000) \\ \frac{n}{2}\cdot \operatorname{log}⁡(2) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000) \\ \frac{n}{2} & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)} \\ n & >\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}≈19.932.
$$

Therefore, the $20$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $1\,000.$
